specAnchors.text: describe the structure of a transformer and understand that a transformer changes the size of an alternating voltage by having different numbers of turns on the input and output sides
explain the use of step-up and step-down transformers in the large-scale generation and transmission of electrical energy

primer.text: Two coils, one iron core, and an alternating input: the transformer rescales an alternating voltage by the turns ratio. This note builds the structure, sorts step-up from step-down, and follows the pair out onto the National Grid, where high voltage means cool cables.

modules.title: Transformer structure and the alternating requirement
modules.opening: A transformer is two coils sharing an iron core: the primary takes the input voltage, the secondary delivers the output, and the core carries the changing field between them. It rescales an alternating voltage — bigger or smaller by the turns ratio — and only alternating works, because a steady field through the secondary would induce nothing.
keyPoints: A transformer has a primary coil, a secondary coil and a shared iron core.
The primary coil is connected to the input alternating voltage.
The changing field in the core threads the secondary coil and induces its output.
A transformer rescales the size of an alternating voltage.
A steady direct input induces nothing in the secondary.

low.restatement: Two coils of wire wrapped on one iron ring. Feed alternating current into the first coil and a changed voltage appears across the second — bigger or smaller depending on the turns.
low.analogy: The core is a conveyor belt for changing fields: the primary places its alternating field on the belt, and the secondary unloads whatever comes round.
low.examPointer: Structure marks need all three parts named — primary coil, secondary coil, iron core — plus the alternating input stated.

medium.restatement: The primary's alternating current makes a continuously changing field in the core; that changing field threads the secondary turn by turn and induces its output voltage, whose size the turns ratio sets. A constant direct current gives a constant core field, so the secondary sees no change and induces nothing — the alternating requirement is the induction trigger, not a design preference.
medium.analogy: A transformer is a relay runner who only passes the baton while it is moving: a runner standing still (steady DC) never hands anything over.
medium.examPointer: If asked why DC fails, answer 'the field through the secondary is not changing, so nothing is induced' — naming the trigger earns the mark.

modules.title: Step-up and step-down transformers
modules.opening: The turns ratio is the transformer's gear lever: more turns on the secondary than the primary steps the voltage up; fewer turns steps it down. Same changing field, same frequency — only the size of the alternating voltage changes, set entirely by the numbers of turns on the two sides.
keyPoints: A step-up transformer has more secondary turns than primary turns and raises the voltage.
A step-down transformer has fewer secondary turns than primary turns and lowers the voltage.
The output size is set by the ratio of turns wound on the two coils.
The output stays alternating at the same frequency as the input.
Equal turns on both sides give an output equal to the input voltage.

low.restatement: Count the turns: more on the output side means the voltage is stepped up; fewer means stepped down; equal means unchanged.
low.analogy: The turns ratio is a gearbox: a big output cog spins the voltage up, a small one winds it down, and equal cogs hold it level.
low.examPointer: Match the names to the turn counts explicitly — 'step-up: more secondary turns' — the pairing is the marked fact.

medium.restatement: Every secondary turn shares the same changing core field, so each turn contributes the same induced voltage increment; the secondary total is that increment times the secondary turn count, while the primary's input sets the per-turn value — hence the output scales with the turns ratio. The transformation alters magnitude only: frequency and alternating character pass through.
medium.analogy: Each secondary turn is one bucket under the same dripping field: ten turns fill ten buckets' worth, one turn fills one.
medium.examPointer: Comparing two transformers: read the turns FIRST, then name step-up or step-down — reversing the pairing loses the mark even with correct working.

modules.title: Transformers on the grid: transmission at high voltage
modules.opening: The National Grid moves energy at very high voltage, and transformers are why: step-up transformers raise the voltage at the power station so the current falls, which slashes the energy lost as heat in the cables. Step-down transformers then lower the voltage safely for homes and factories.
keyPoints: Step-up transformers raise the voltage before electricity is transmitted across the grid.
At higher transmission voltage the cable current is lower for the same power.
A lower cable current wastes less energy as heat in the cables.
Step-down transformers lower the voltage for safe local use.
The transformer pair — step-up then step-down — brackets the long transmission lines.

low.restatement: Power stations step the voltage UP for the long journey, so less energy is wasted heating the cables; near your home it is stepped DOWN to a safe level.
low.analogy: It is like carrying water in a narrow pipe: pump at high pressure (voltage) so only a thin flow (current) is needed, and little is lost to friction on the way.
low.examPointer: Transmission answers need the chain: higher voltage → lower current → less heat loss. Quoting only 'high voltage' misses the reasoning.

medium.restatement: For a fixed transmitted power, raising the voltage proportionally lowers the current; cable heating scales with the square of the current, so the saving compounds at every voltage increase. Step-up transformers make the high-voltage transmission possible and step-down units restore safe levels at the consumer end — the 6.18P role split between the two transformer families.
medium.analogy: High-voltage transmission is carpooling for energy: pack the same passengers (power) into fewer vehicles (current) so the road (cable) heats up far less.
medium.examPointer: Use the word 'heat' or 'wasted energy' with 'lower current' — 'less resistance' is wrong: the cable is unchanged; only the current differs.

glossary.definition: A primary coil, secondary coil and iron core that change the size of an alternating voltage.
A transformer with more secondary than primary turns that raises the voltage.
A transformer with fewer secondary than primary turns that lowers the voltage.
